title: Topotijdreis / historical topographic map series, 1815-2025
license: Dutch government open data (TOPraster GeoTIFFs via PDOK)
projection: true plan, published georeferenced in EPSG:28992 - NO fitting required
georef_notes: The one source in this catalogue needing no georeferencing: the tile grid IS EPSG:28992 (origin -30515500.0 / 31112399.999999993; LOD 11 = 1.5875 m/px is the finest published). Substitute any year 1815-2025 into the service name. The host MOVED - the old services.arcgisonline.nl 'Historisch' folder 404s and that server no longer has the folder.
notes: 1815 is a REGIONAL engraving, useless for buildings: the whole town is a ~400 px blob under Zuiderzee hatching. Colour begins in 1880, whose full-colour Bonneblad prints buildings in carmine - that is what scripts/extract-map-blocks.py segments. Roads use the SAME carmine, so they are rejected by shape, not colour. Years are validity ranges, not surveys: 1880/1885/1890/1895/1898 return byte-identical tiles, as do 1870/1872/1875. At 1.5875 m/px this yields blocks, never individual houses.

title: Van Deventer, 1545
license: map itself public domain (age); scan rights not yet checked
orientation: North up, east right - unambiguous: the sheet is labelled Septentrio (top), Meridies (bottom), Oriens (right), Occidens (left).
scale_bar: "Passus quingentum" bar on the main sheet, ticks at 100/200/300/400/500 passus. Not yet measured in pixels.
georef_notes: TRUE planimetric plan - streets, blocks and the moat are drawn flat; only churches and gates appear as small pictorial symbols. Van Deventer surveyed the Netherlandish cities for Philip II, so these are the earliest systematic true-plan surveys of Dutch towns. Best first georeferencing target of the pre-1811 set: oldest AND most geometrically faithful. The scan is a two-page atlas spread (Biblioteca Nacional de Espana) with a book gutter; the left inset panel shows the city at larger scale than the right-hand regional sheet - prefer the inset for the city itself.
notes: Earliest plan in the kwaad.net overview. Scanned image only, no vector/geo data. PROVENANCE (per the user, worth confirming against the literature): Van Deventer surveyed streets and facade widths in the field and re-measured them himself several times, so the STREET WIDTHS and FACADE WIDTHS on these plans are measured quantities. House DEPTHS and garden/yard depths are the surveyor's own guesswork. That maps directly onto what this project should trust: use them as evidence for frontage and street geometry, never for plot depth. Facade TYPE as drawn may also be reliable.

title: Van Deventer, 1560
license: map itself public domain (age); scan rights not yet checked
orientation: North up, east right - unambiguous: the regional sheet is labelled "Noordt" (top), "West" (left), "Oost" (right), and the Zuiderzee occupies the bottom edge.
georef_notes: TRUE planimetric plan, and the clearest of the pre-1600 set: streets, canals, blocks and the moat all drawn flat, buildings as red roof-plan masses, only churches as small symbols. Two images: the full regional sheet (02AA) covering several km of countryside with Hoorn small in the lower middle, and a high-resolution detail crop of the city itself (uitsnede) - prefer the detail crop for tracing the city. The regional sheet also names surrounding settlements still on the map today (Zwaag, Blokker, the Reguliers monastery, a leper house west of town), which are candidate control points for fitting the wide sheet. Provenance: the scan is a 19th-century lithographic facsimile ("JACOB VAN DEVENTER, del." / "Lith. J. Smulders & Co., Den Haag"), not the original manuscript - facsimile redrawing is a possible extra error source to keep in mind when residuals are assessed.
notes: PROVENANCE (per the user, worth confirming against the literature): Van Deventer surveyed streets and facade widths in the field and re-measured them himself several times, so the STREET WIDTHS and FACADE WIDTHS on these plans are measured quantities. House DEPTHS and garden/yard depths are the surveyor's own guesswork. That maps directly onto what this project should trust: use them as evidence for frontage and street geometry, never for plot depth. Facade TYPE as drawn may also be reliable.

title: Guicciardini, 1582
license: map itself public domain (age); scan rights not yet checked
orientation: North at the bottom, water at the top - same convention as Blaeu 1649: the Zuiderzee with ships fills the top edge, and Hoorn sits on its south/south-west shore.
georef_notes: NOT a true plan. Titled "Hoorn in Hollandt". Buildings drawn as 3D houses and the surrounding fields drawn receding into the distance, so the ground plan is foreshortened - a similarity (rotate+scale) fit is invalid, same as Blaeu 1649. Shares its viewpoint, framing and the Neptune-on-a-sea-monster cartouche with Utenwael 1596; the two are clearly the same view family (one derived from the other or both from a common source), so they are not independent evidence. Use for street layout, block structure, fortification form and building existence - not for footprint geometry.

title: Utenwael, 1596
license: map itself public domain (age); scan rights not yet checked
orientation: North at the bottom, water at the top - same convention as Guicciardini 1582 and Blaeu 1649.
georef_notes: NOT a true plan. Titled "Hoorn in Westfrijslandt 1596", signed "PAVLVS VTEN WAEL F". Buildings drawn as 3D houses in oblique view; same caveats as Guicciardini 1582, with which it shares viewpoint, framing and the Neptune cartouche - treat the two as one view family rather than independent sources. Higher engraving detail than Guicciardini, so it is the better of the two for reading street layout and fortification detail.

title: Blaeu, 1649
license: map itself public domain (age); scan rights not yet checked
orientation: North at the BOTTOM, east at the LEFT (~4 deg off a straight 180-degree rotation). Confirmed two ways: the compass rose needle runs top->bottom, and the open water full of ships along the top edge is the Zuiderzee, which lies south/south-east of Hoorn.
scale_bar: "Virgae Rhijnlandicae", ticks at 0/10/20/30/40/50 roeden. Measured 3.54 px per roede at 1500px-wide scan; 1 Rijnlandse roede = 3.767 m, giving ~1.06 m/px along the bar.
georef_notes: NOT a true plan - do not fit with a similarity (rotate+scale) transform. Measured evidence: the walled city occupies roughly 1240x580 px on the scan (ratio ~2.1), while the real pre-1700 built-up area measures 975x799 m (ratio 1.22) from BAG footprints; the implied scale differs per axis (~0.79 vs ~1.38 m/px). The view is foreshortened by roughly 1.7x, and buildings are drawn as 3D houses, so roof/facade parallax displaces footprints further. Usable for street layout, block structure and which buildings existed; needs at minimum a projective/affine fit with 4+ control points, and footprint precision stays limited. HIGH-RESOLUTION SCAN FOUND: Rijksmuseum RP-P-AO-7-36-1A via Wikimedia Commons, 5978x4966 (29.7 MP) against the 1500x1193 (1.8 MP) kwaad.net copy - roughly 3x linear on the map area. At that resolution individual gabled houses are countable and the street names are legible on the plate itself ("Kerck Straet", "Nieu Straet", "t Oost", "Ouden Noort", "Nieuwen Noort"), which identifies streets directly instead of by inference. This makes Blaeu the PRIMARY source for the house-sequence method (see data/historic-streets/README.md), despite being useless for whole-scan georeferencing.
notes: Named as a candidate first pre-1811 map to georeference in the phase-3 roadmap - well-known, detailed town atlas plan.

title: Het ontstaan van Hoorn (Vereniging Oud Hoorn / Archeologie West-Friesland)
publisher: Vereniging Oud Hoorn, reconstructions by Archeologie West-Friesland
license: not stated - contact Vereniging Oud Hoorn before republishing; used here as reference only
georef_notes: ontstaanHoorn4.jpg is the single most useful item found so far: a 4887x3323 scan of the Van Deventer 1560 plan (~3.3x the kwaad.net uitsnede) with the 1275 infrastructure overlaid by Archeologie West-Friesland - brown Omringdijk, green Dam, blue Waterloop - and a marker disc on the Roode Steen. The disc gives a control point with no guesswork, and the dike is documented as following the Kleine Oost / Grote Oost / Roode Steen / het West line, all of which are still modern street names and therefore geocodable. ontstaanHoorn1-3 are reconstructions of the cultural landscape at 1250 and 1275.
notes: Also references a "Maquette van Hoorn 1650" (physical scale model) via the Oud Hoorn beeldbank - an existing 3D reconstruction of the city worth investigating for the modelling phase. Note: the site 404s for non-browser user agents on some paths, and web.archive.org is blocked by this environment's egress policy.
